concepts.name: Kyoto Protocol: Legal Architecture and UNFCCC Relationship
key_dimensions: Kyoto Protocol as an 'operationalizing instrument' under UNFCCC — not a standalone treaty
Distinction between UNFCCC parties and Kyoto Protocol parties (USA signed UNFCCC but not KP)
CMP (Conference of Parties serving as Meeting of Parties) vs COP — overlapping yet distinct governance
Legal bindingness of emission targets under KP vs. voluntary NDCs under Paris Agreement

concepts.name: Annex I vs Non-Annex I Country Classification
key_dimensions: Annex I: industrialized + economies-in-transition (EIT) countries bearing binding targets
Non-Annex I: developing nations with no binding reduction targets — India, China included
UPSC trap: Annex I ≠ Annex B (Annex B specifically lists quantified emission limits under KP)
Common but Differentiated Responsibilities (CBDR) principle as the legal basis for this distinction

concepts.name: Annex B and Quantified Emission Limitation/Reduction Objectives (QELROs)
key_dimensions: Annex B lists specific percentage reduction targets for each Annex I party relative to 1990 baseline
Distinction: Annex B is KP-specific; Annex I belongs to UNFCCC — overlap but not identical membership
EU bubble arrangement: EU-15 allowed collective target fulfillment under burden-sharing agreement
Countries like Australia and Iceland were allowed emission increases under Annex B

concepts.name: Clean Development Mechanism (CDM): Structure and Functioning
key_dimensions: Only KP mechanism that directly involves Non-Annex I (developing) countries
Generates Certified Emission Reductions (CERs) — 1 CER = 1 tonne CO₂ equivalent avoided
Dual objective: Annex I compliance + sustainable development in host (developing) country
CDM Executive Board under CMP — supranational oversight body; Designated National Authorities (DNA) at country level

concepts.name: CDM Project Cycle and Additionality Principle
key_dimensions: Additionality: emission reductions must be 'additional' to what would occur without the CDM project
Steps: PDD → DOE validation → CDM EB registration → monitoring → DOE verification → CER issuance
Designated Operational Entities (DOEs) — third-party auditors; UPSC trap: not government bodies
Controversy: 'hot air' credits and perverse incentives (HFC-23 destruction scandal)

concepts.name: Joint Implementation (JI): Mechanism and ERU Generation
key_dimensions: Operates exclusively between Annex I parties (unlike CDM which involves Non-Annex I)
Generates Emission Reduction Units (ERUs) — 1 ERU = 1 tonne CO₂ equivalent
ERUs converted from host country's Assigned Amount Units (AAUs), ensuring no double-counting
Track 1 (host country verifies, simpler) vs Track 2 (JISC oversight, stricter) — UPSC trap distinction

concepts.name: International Emissions Trading (IET): AAU-based Carbon Market
key_dimensions: Annex I parties can trade Assigned Amount Units (AAUs) among themselves
UPSC trap: IET is government-to-government trading; EU ETS is a separate regional scheme not mandated by KP
'Hot air' problem: Russia/Ukraine had surplus AAUs due to economic collapse post-1990 baseline
Supplementarity principle: Kyoto mechanisms must be 'supplemental' to domestic action — no quantified cap defined

concepts.name: The Four Kyoto Units: AAU, CER, ERU, RMU
key_dimensions: AAU (Assigned Amount Unit): baseline allocation to Annex B parties; ERU (Joint Implementation); CER (CDM); RMU (Land Use)
Removal Unit (RMU): generated from LULUCF activities (afforestation, reforestation) — cannot be banked to second commitment period
UPSC trap: All units are fungible (1 unit = 1 tonne CO₂e) but have different banking/carry-over rules
Registries and ITL (International Transaction Log) — UNFCCC secretariat tracks all unit transfers

concepts.name: LULUCF (Land Use, Land-Use Change and Forestry) under Kyoto
key_dimensions: Article 3.3: mandatory accounting for afforestation, reforestation, deforestation since 1990
Article 3.4: optional additional activities (forest management, cropland, grazing land management)
Generates RMUs — sinks can offset emissions but RMUs have restricted banking unlike CERs/AAUs
Controversy: forest management credits allowed countries to claim large sink credits (Canada, Russia benefited)

concepts.name: Kyoto Protocol Commitment Periods: First and Second
key_dimensions: First Commitment Period: 2008–2012; average 5.2% reduction below 1990 levels for Annex I
Doha Amendment (2012): established Second Commitment Period 2013–2020; 18% reduction target
UPSC trap: Doha Amendment never formally entered into force (needed 144 ratifications, achieved only in 2020 — after Paris Agreement already operative)
Canada withdrew from KP in 2011; USA never ratified; Japan, Russia, New Zealand opted out of 2nd period

concepts.name: USA's Non-Ratification and Its Systemic Implications
key_dimensions: USA signed KP in 1998 (Clinton) but Senate passed Byrd-Hagel Resolution (1997) blocking ratification
Byrd-Hagel: objected to absence of binding targets for major developing economies like China and India
USA remained UNFCCC party but not KP party — could observe CMP but not vote
UPSC trap: USA's absence ≠ withdrawal; withdrawal requires being a party first (like Canada in 2011)

concepts.name: Marrakesh Accords (COP-7, 2001): Operationalizing KP Mechanisms
key_dimensions: Translated KP's legal text into operational rules for CDM, JI, and IET
Established CDM Executive Board, JI Supervisory Committee, Compliance Committee
Defined eligibility requirements for participating in flexible mechanisms (national registries, annual inventories)
UPSC trap: Marrakesh Accords adopted in 2001 but KP entered into force only in 2005 — gap between rules and legal effect

concepts.name: Compliance Mechanism under the Kyoto Protocol
key_dimensions: Two-branch system: Facilitative Branch (assistance/advice) and Enforcement Branch (consequences for non-compliance)
Enforcement Branch can impose 1.3× penalty ratio — must make up shortfall × 1.3 in next period
Suspension from IET for non-compliant parties — financial incentive for compliance
UPSC trap: KP compliance mechanism is legally binding for Annex I parties; contrast with Paris Agreement's 'name and shame' facilitative mechanism

concepts.name: KP vs Paris Agreement: Architectural Comparison
key_dimensions: KP: top-down binding targets for Annex I only; Paris: bottom-up NDCs for all parties (universal)
KP baseline: 1990; Paris: no fixed baseline — countries choose their own reference years
KP mechanisms (CDM/JI/IET) vs Paris Article 6 mechanisms (cooperative approaches, SDM, non-market approaches)
UPSC trap: Paris Agreement does not replace KP — KP's second commitment period (Doha) and Paris coexist; Article 6 of Paris is not yet CDM's formal successor

concepts.name: Article 6 of Paris Agreement and Transition from CDM
key_dimensions: Article 6.2: bilateral cooperative approaches generating Internationally Transferred Mitigation Outcomes (ITMOs)
Article 6.4: Sustainable Development Mechanism (SDM) — CDM's successor; supervised by Article 6.4 body
Glasgow (COP-26, 2021): rules for Article 6 finalized; CDM credits transition — only post-2013 CERs eligible
UPSC trap: Article 6 of Paris ≠ CDM; SDM open to all parties, not just Annex I buying from Non-Annex I

concepts.name: Basket of Six Greenhouse Gases under Kyoto Protocol
key_dimensions: CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, HFCs, PFCs, SF₆ — regulated under KP's first commitment period
NF₃ (nitrogen trifluoride) added in second commitment period (Doha Amendment)
Global Warming Potential (GWP) used to convert all gases to CO₂ equivalent for accounting
UPSC trap: ozone-depleting substances (CFCs) regulated under Montreal Protocol, NOT Kyoto Protocol — common confusion

concepts.name: India's Position and Benefits under Kyoto Protocol
key_dimensions: India is Non-Annex I — no binding targets; significant CDM host country (2nd largest after China)
India's CDM projects primarily in renewable energy, energy efficiency, and waste management sectors
Designated National Authority (DNA) in India: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
UPSC trap: India benefited financially from CDM but this did not imply acceptance of binding targets — CBDR principle maintained

concepts.name: Economies in Transition (EIT) and Special Provisions
key_dimensions: EIT countries (Russia, Eastern Europe) given flexibility on base year — some could use years other than 1990
Russia's ratification in 2004 was critical — triggered KP's entry into force (55% of Annex I emissions threshold)
UPSC trap: KP's entry into force required 55 parties AND 55% of Annex I 1990 emissions — dual threshold
Russia later refused second commitment period, joining Canada, Japan, New Zealand in opting out

concepts.name: Supplementarity Principle and Domestic Action Requirement
key_dimensions: KP Article 17 and Marrakesh Accords state mechanisms must be 'supplemental' to domestic action
No quantified cap on how much of a target can be met through mechanisms — political compromise
EU internally imposed stricter supplementarity caps; other parties (Canada) relied heavily on credits
UPSC trap: supplementarity is a qualitative obligation, not a quantified limit — frequently tested as a misconception

concepts.name: Gold Standard and Co-Benefits in CDM
key_dimensions: Gold Standard: voluntary premium certification for CDM projects delivering strong sustainable development co-benefits
Developed by WWF and NGOs — not an official UNFCCC/CDM standard but widely recognized
Commands premium CER prices; focuses on renewable energy and efficiency projects, excludes industrial gas projects
UPSC relevance: illustrates tension between carbon offsetting (quantity) and sustainable development quality in climate finance
